chunks: "For the inductor, the minimum comes from ripple and from the controller.
If L is too small, ripple current gets large, so peak current hits the current limit, RMS current and core loss rise, output ripple grows, and at light load the converter drops into DCM.
On peak-current-mode parts there's also a minimum from slope compensation, because the inductor down-slope V OUT over L must be below what the ramp can handle.
The maximum comes from transient response and the physical part.
A big L slows the current slew, V over L , so on a load step the output capacitor has to carry the load for longer and the droop gets worse.
It also pushes the LC corner down which squeezes loop bandwidth, and a bigger inductor at a given size has a lower saturation current or higher DCR.
For the capacitor, the minimum is set by ripple, by the load-transient droop, and by what the compensation needs for phase margin. The maximum is mostly start-up and loop.
The charging current C dV over dt during soft-start has to stay under the current limit or you trip into hiccup, large C slows the control loop, and the datasheet usually lists a max.
So L and C each have a window, and I pick values in the middle."
